title: Harsha Crowned at Sixteen
text: In 606 CE a 16-year-old prince named Harsha was crowned after his elder brother was assassinated. He later declared himself ruler of Kannauj and moved his capital there, ruling a large empire in northern India until 647. A poet himself, he wrote three Sanskrit plays and sponsored the chronicler Bana, whose "Deeds of Harsha" tells the story of his early career.

title: A Port Mosque at the Indus Mouth
text: On a creek 65 km east of Karachi lie the ruins of Banbhore, the region's best-preserved medieval port. Its stone mosque, whose prayer hall roof rested on 33 wooden pillars, carries an inscription dated 727 AD, about 16 years after Muhammad Bin Qasim's Arab conquest of Sindh. Beside the town, workshops processed textiles and made glass, glazes and metal goods.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Port of Banbhore (Tentative List)

title: Vikramashila, City of Monks
text: Tibetan tradition says the Pala king Dharmapala founded the great monastery of Vikramashila, built from the early 9th century at Antichak in Bihar. Excavators found a vast square monastery with about 208 cells, each with its own bed platform. It was famous for Tantric Buddhism, and one Tibetan writer, Taranatha, says a thousand monks lived there permanently.

title: A Zero Carved in Stone
text: Inside a temple at Gwalior is an inscription that uses a round "0" in recording a measurement of land. In 1883 the German scholar Eugen Hultzsch copied and translated it, dating the text to 876 CE. For a long time it was counted as the oldest known zero used as a placeholder in India, until carbon dating showed the Bakhshali manuscript was older.

source.name: Scientific American: The Elusive Origin of Zero

source2.name: University of Oxford GLAM: Carbon dating finds Bakhshali manuscript contains oldest recorded origins of the symbol 'zero'

title: Prithviraja's Last Battle
text: In 1191 the Rajput king Prithviraja III beat the army of Muhammad Ghuri at Taraori, about 110 km north of Delhi. Ghuri returned in 1192 with a stronger army, using mounted archers to lure Prithviraja's men out of line before heavy cavalry struck. Prithviraja was captured and executed, and Muslim control of northern India followed within a generation.

title: Raising the Qutb Minar
text: From 1199 Delhi's new Muslim rulers raised a minaret beside the Quwwatu'l-Islam, the oldest mosque in northern India, built partly of materials reused from some 20 temples. Made of red and buff sandstone carved with bands of inscriptions, the Qutb Minar stands 72.5 metres high, the tallest masonry tower in India, with balconies for the call to prayer.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi

title: A Sultan's Tomb Goes to a Saint
text: Between 1320 and 1324 the Tughluq ruler Ghiyas-ud-din built a great octagonal tomb at Multan, probably meant for his own dynasty. Instead it was given to the family of the Sufi saint Shah Rukn-i-Alam. The 35-metre red-brick tomb is framed with shisham wood beams and decorated with blue and white tiles, and over 100,000 pilgrims still visit it.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam (Tentative List)

title: A Traveller Becomes Delhi's Judge
text: Hearing that Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq of Delhi was generous to Muslim scholars, the traveller Ibn Battuta headed for India and, by his own dating, reached the Indus on September 12, 1333. The sultan made him grand qadi, or judge, of Delhi. But the ruler mixed generosity with cruelty, and Ibn Battuta feared daily for his life until he left as an envoy to China.

title: Bengal's Giant Adina Mosque
text: In 1373 Sikandar Shah, son of Iliyas Shah, built the Adina Mosque at Pandua in Bengal. Banglapedia calls it the largest mosque of medieval times in the whole subcontinent, about 155 by 87 metres on the outside. Estimates of its domes range from 260 to 370, and a raised stone platform was probably a royal gallery for the ruler at prayer.

title: Nimai, the Singing Saint
text: In 1486, on the night of a lunar eclipse, a boy named Vishvambhara Mishra, nicknamed Nimai, was born in Navadvipa, Bengal. As Chaitanya, he inspired devotional singing and dancing that became nightly gatherings in a neighbour's courtyard, then spilled into the streets, once causing a clash with the local qazi. He later lived in Puri until his death in 1533.

title: Pema Lingpa's Temple of Dances
text: In 1501 Pema Lingpa, Bhutan's famous "treasure revealer", built Tamzhing monastery in Bumthang. He was also skilled in metalwork and in carving wooden blocks for printing scriptures. Tamzhing is known for its unique wall paintings and is the original home of sacred dances now performed at tshechu festivals throughout Bhutan. Pema Lingpa died there in 1521, aged seventy-two.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Tamzhing Monastery (Tentative List)

title: A Mughal Princess Heads for Mecca
text: In October 1576 Emperor Akbar stood beside his aunt Gulbadan, aged 53, at Fatehpur Sikri to bid her farewell. She was leading eleven other senior women of the royal household on pilgrimage to Mecca. Their route ran first to Surat, the docking port in Gujarat, and poorer pilgrims were given free passage on the Mughal ships under state policy.

source.name: Yale University Press: The Mughal Princess Who Led a Pilgrimage to Mecca (excerpt by Ruby Lal)

title: A Turkey Amazes the Emperor
text: In 1612 a shipment of exotic birds and animals gathered at the port of Cambay caused a sensation at Emperor Jahangir's court. Among them was a North American turkey. Jahangir wrote that its head and neck kept changing colour, "like a chameleon", and ordered it painted. The court artist Mansur, honoured as "Wonder of the Age", made the portrait.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Painting of a turkey cock, Mansur, ca. 1612

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Painting of a cheer pheasant, Mansur, ca. 1620

title: Escape in a Basket of Sweets
text: Forced to make peace, the Maratha leader Shivaji came to Emperor Aurangzeb's court at Agra, where he and his son were put under house arrest under threat of execution. Shivaji pretended to be ill and, as a penance, sent out huge baskets of sweets for the poor. On August 17, 1666, he and his son had themselves carried past the guards inside them.

title: Dhaka's Unlucky Unfinished Fort
text: In 1678 Prince Muhammad Azam, Mughal viceroy of Bengal, began a palace fortress at Dhaka, today called Lalbagh Fort or Fort Aurangabad. Aurangzeb recalled him before it was finished. The next governor, Shaista Khan, never restarted the work: his daughter Bibi Pari, the "Lady Fairy", died there in 1684, and he came to see the site as unlucky.

title: Five Beloved Ones at Anandpur
text: On Baisakhi Day in 1699 a large crowd of Sikhs gathered at Anandpur. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh came out of a tent with a drawn sword and asked who would give his life for the faith. Five men stepped forward, one by one. They became the panj pyare, the first initiated into the Khalsa with sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword.

title: Jaipur, a City on a Grid
text: In 1727 Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur. Unlike other cities in the region, set in hilly terrain, it was laid out on a plain to a grid plan interpreted through Vedic architecture. Colonnaded shops line its main streets, which meet at large public squares called chaupars. It was designed as a commercial capital, and its craft traditions continue today.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Jaipur City, Rajasthan

title: Marathas and Afghans at Panipat
text: On January 14, 1761, a Maratha army under Sadashiv Rao Bhau, weakened by disease and shortage of money, marched out of its fortified camp at Panipat against Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghans. The Marathas did well at first, but late in the afternoon about 5,000 fresh Afghan cavalry turned the battle. Estimates of the dead range from 60,000 to 70,000.

title: The Day the Coast Rose
text: On April 2, 1762, a great earthquake struck violently from Dhaka along the Meghna River to Chittagong. Parts of offshore islands rose as much as 6.71 metres, while 155.4 square kilometres near Chittagong sank for good. Rivers surged, a large river dried up, and 500 people died in Dhaka. Two volcanoes were even said to have opened in the Sitakunda hills.

title: A Judge Finds Long-Lost Language Cousins
text: Sir William Jones, who learned 28 languages in his life, sailed for Calcutta in 1783 as a supreme court judge and in 1784 founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal. He took up Sanskrit for his work on law. In his 1786 presidential talk to the Society he proposed that Sanskrit, Latin and Greek shared a common ancestry, spurring the new field of comparative linguistics.

title: The Lion of the Punjab Takes Lahore
text: In July 1799 the Sikh chief Ranjit Singh seized Lahore, capital of the Punjab. The Afghan king Zaman Shah confirmed him as governor, but in 1801 he proclaimed himself maharaja and struck coins in the name of the Sikh Gurus. Blind in one eye, he went on to push back Afghan power and became known as the Lion of the Punjab.
